items.question: An enterprise IT service desk routes tickets: a classifier decides whether each goes to a cheap fast model or to the higher-capability one. Routing cut cost by 45%. The post-deployment audit shows quality of 0.79 on the cheap path against 0.91 on the capable path, with overall quality four points below the pre-routing baseline. The team proposes moving the lowest-scoring ticket categories permanently to the capable model. Which analysis should precede that decision?

options.A: Re-tune the classifier's confidence threshold so more tickets go to the capable path, then measure the resulting quality and cost and iterate from there.
options.B: Compare the cheap path's score against the pre-routing baseline restricted to the same ticket categories, to establish how large the loss on that path really is before deciding how much of the 45% saving is worth giving back.
options.C: Increase the audit sample until the twelve-point gap between the two paths reaches statistical significance at the team's chosen confidence level.
options.D: Score the cheap model on the tickets the router sent it and, separately, on a sample the router sent to the capable path, separating the cheap model's capability from the router's allocation decisions.

items.question: A marketing platform's subject-line generator showed a clear offline win: the candidate prompt beat the incumbent by six points on a 600-case model-graded suite, well outside the interval. A four-week 50/50 online test across 2.3 million sends, with assignment fixed per recipient for the whole test, shows no difference in open rate. Nothing in the serving stack differs between the arms except the prompt. (Choose THREE.) Which three explanations are consistent with all of the evidence given?

options.A: The online test was underpowered, because four weeks is too short a window for an email experiment to resolve a difference of this kind.
options.B: The judge rubric rewards properties of a subject line that have no influence on whether a recipient opens the message.
options.C: The offline suite's case mix does not match the send mix, so the categories where the candidate wins may be a small share of real sends.
options.D: The arms interfered with each other, because a recipient could receive sends generated by both prompts over the four weeks.
options.E: Open rate is driven mainly by sender, timing and list quality, so the subject line's contribution is small enough that a genuine improvement in it need not register.

items.question: A game publisher's player-support agent holds sessions that often run for hours. To control cost the team added context compaction: once a session passes a token threshold, earlier turns are replaced by a running summary. Spend per session fell 30%. The single-turn eval suite is unchanged, and the production audit — which samples individual responses uniformly across all traffic and scores them — is also unchanged. Player complaints that the agent 'forgets what I told it' have tripled. Which diagnostic localises the effect using data the team already holds?

options.A: Re-slice the existing audit scores by player tier, since complaint volume is concentrated among the most engaged players and the effect should be visible there.
options.B: Grade each running summary against the turns it replaced, using a fixed checklist of facts a player has stated, to establish how much information the summariser drops at each compaction step and whether the loss grows with session length.
options.C: Re-slice the existing audit scores by each response's position relative to the first compaction event in its session, since a uniform sample over responses is dominated by short sessions in which compaction never fires.
options.D: Re-run the single-turn eval suite against the compacted and uncompacted pipelines with a larger sample, to detect a smaller effect than the current suite can resolve.

items.question: An LLM feature degrades in output quality with no change in error rate, latency or throughput. Which class of monitoring can detect this, and why?

options.A: Continuous sampled scoring of production outputs, because a confidently wrong answer is indistinguishable from a correct one in any signal derived from the transport or the runtime.
options.B: Anomaly detection over request and response volumes, because degraded generations shift the response length distribution and the retry pattern before any other symptom of the change becomes visible to operators.
options.C: Synthetic canary requests replayed hourly, because they confirm that the endpoint keeps returning well-formed responses inside the latency budget.
options.D: Distributed tracing across the chain, because a quality loss localises to whichever stage's span duration has changed relative to its baseline.

items.question: A biotech platform team is told to cut roughly a quarter from its evaluation spend, which is dominated by judge-model calls. The portfolio is: a 60-case blocking gate on every merge; a 2,000-case nightly full suite; a weekly 5,000-case quality-trend report circulated to leadership, which is the second-largest line item; and a 500-case adversarial suite run before each release. Which reduction preserves the most decision value?

options.A: Cut the nightly full suite to weekly, since the merge gate already runs on every change and the nightly run largely repeats coverage the gate has already provided, at seven times the frequency and cost.
options.B: Reduce the merge gate to a smaller subset and run the full gate only before a release, since most merges do not reach production immediately.
options.C: Reduce the trend report to a smaller stratified sample on a monthly cadence, leaving the merge gate, the nightly suite and the pre-release adversarial suite intact.
options.D: Run the adversarial suite on alternate releases, since adversarial cases change slowly and the suite rarely alters a release decision.

items.question: A mortgage servicer scores 200 randomly sampled production responses a day with a model judge. The long-run pass rate is 92%. The team proposes paging the on-call engineer whenever a day's pass rate comes in 2 points or more below 92%. What is the problem with that threshold?

options.A: The threshold is too loose: on 200 items a 2-point shortfall is far outside sampling noise, so genuine degradations smaller than that will run for weeks without anyone being paged.
options.B: It conflates the grader's error rate with the system's, so the on-call will be paged whenever the judge is miscalibrated rather than when quality has actually fallen.
options.C: A pass rate is a proportion, so a fixed percentage-point threshold is not a valid alerting rule; the condition has to be expressed as an odds ratio against the baseline.
options.D: Day-to-day sampling noise on 200 items has a standard deviation of about 2 points, so a 2-point shortfall is roughly a one-sigma event and will page on about one day in seven with nothing wrong.

items.question: A grain trading firm's market-note generator began producing notes with stale price references at 06:00. The team rolled back the only change in the window — a prompt release from the previous evening — at 07:20. Two hours later the stale references persist at the same rate. The model version is pinned, the running prompt is byte-identical to the version that ran correctly for three weeks, and the service has been restarted. What is the next step?

options.A: Verify what the generator is actually reading: check the freshness and identity of the price data returned at request time, since the inputs are now the only thing that differs from the known-good state.
options.B: Roll back one release further, on the basis that the previous evening's release may not have been the first change to introduce the behaviour and that the three-week-old prompt may itself contain a defect that only manifested once prices moved.
options.C: Re-run the regression suite against the restored prompt to confirm that the rollback was correctly applied to every serving instance.
options.D: Raise an incident with the model provider, since a pinned version is now the only component left that could have changed underneath the service.

items.question: A streaming service pre-registered a rollout rule before canarying a cheaper model on its recommendation-explanation feature: ship only if the candidate's quality loss against the incumbent is below 1 point with 95% confidence. The canary has run its planned two weeks. The observed loss is 0.6 points, with a 95% confidence interval on the loss running from -0.7 to 1.9 points, where a negative loss means the candidate scored higher. Cost modelling shows a meaningful monthly saving. The product director wants to ship, citing the 0.6 figure. What does the pre-registered rule require here?

options.A: The rule is met: the estimated loss of 0.6 points is below the 1-point bar, and the width of the interval reflects the sample size rather than the size of the effect.
options.B: The rule is not met: the data remain consistent with a loss above 1 point, so shipping requires either more canary data to tighten the interval or an explicit, recorded decision to override the rule.
options.C: The rule is not met and the candidate must be rejected, because an interval extending beyond the bar is evidence that the candidate is worse than the incumbent by more than the tolerance, and a rule that two weeks of canary could not satisfy will not be satisfied later.
options.D: The rule cannot be applied, because a confidence interval on a difference in judge scores is not a statement about quality in the sense the rule was written to capture.

items.question: A pharmaceutical company's medical-information assistant answers clinician queries from an approved document set. Accuracy on the weekly audit fell over three weeks. Two things changed inside that window: the provider alias the service resolves moved to a newer model version, and the monthly document-set refresh ran. Both the previous model version and the pre-refresh document snapshot are still available. (Choose TWO.) Which two observations would together establish that the document refresh, rather than the model change, is responsible?

options.A: The refreshed document set is substantially larger than the previous one, and larger corpora reduce retrieval precision at a fixed top-k.
options.B: Replaying the failing queries against the previous model version with the current document set reproduces the failures at the same rate.
options.C: Re-scoring an archived sample of pre-window outputs with today's judge returns the same scores those outputs originally received.
options.D: Replaying the failing queries against the current model version with the pre-refresh document snapshot restores accuracy to its earlier level.
options.E: Latency and token usage per query are unchanged across the three weeks, indicating that the pipeline is structurally the same as before.

items.question: In an AI incident postmortem, what distinguishes a finding that belongs in the regression suite from one that belongs in production monitoring?

options.A: Correctness findings belong in the regression suite and safety findings belong in monitoring, because adversarial behaviour cannot be enumerated in advance as test cases.
options.B: Findings from customer-reported incidents belong in the regression suite and findings from internal audits belong in monitoring, matching each control to the audience that raised it and to the severity that the reporting route implies.
options.C: A finding with a reproducible input that triggers it becomes a test case; a finding that depends on live conditions such as traffic mix, load or upstream data becomes a monitored signal with an alert.
options.D: Findings that have recurred at least twice belong in the regression suite, while a single occurrence is monitored until a second one justifies the cost of writing a test.

items.question: A customs brokerage classifies commodity codes with Claude, two million classifications a month. Configuration A costs $0.020 per classification and is correct 91% of the time; configuration B costs $0.012 and is correct 84%. Every incorrect classification is caught downstream by a licensed broker and reworked at an average internal cost of $0.90. A cost review recommends B on the grounds that it is cheaper per correct answer. What is the correct reading?

options.A: The review is right: B costs about $0.0143 per correct answer against A's $0.0220, and rework sits in operations rather than in the platform's budget, so it does not belong in a comparison of configurations.
options.B: Neither figure is decisive, because cost per correct answer and cost including rework rank the two configurations the same way, so the choice should be made on latency instead.
options.C: The two configurations differ by less than the uncertainty in the 91% and 84% accuracy estimates, so a confidence interval on accuracy is needed before any cost conclusion can be drawn.
options.D: The per-correct figure is arithmetically right but incomplete: including rework, A costs $0.101 per classification against B's $0.156, making B about $110,000 a month more expensive.

items.question: An online learning platform runs a Claude writing tutor for 300,000 students. Product has committed to 1.5s to first token; the team currently keeps all safety rules in the system prompt and is adding a dedicated input moderation classifier. Measurements show the classifier adds roughly 180ms when run before generation, which pushes the p95 over budget on the slowest region. An engineer proposes running the classifier and the generation call concurrently. What is the sound way to implement that?

options.A: Keep the classifier strictly before generation, because running the two concurrently necessarily trades safety for latency and there is no design that recovers the gate.
options.B: Run both concurrently and begin streaming immediately, terminating the stream the moment the classifier flags the input; almost all requests are benign, so few students would ever see content that is later withdrawn.
options.C: Drop the input classifier and rely on the output classifier alone, since a harmful input only matters when it produces a harmful output, and the output check already sits in the delivery path.
options.D: Dispatch the classifier and the generation call concurrently, but withhold the first streamed token until the classifier verdict returns.

items.question: An energy utility runs a public outage assistant with two paths: a status lookup that returns deterministic data from the outage database, and a free-text path that answers safety questions such as what to do about a suspected gas smell. Both paths pass through the same third-party moderation classifier. During a storm the classifier's p99 latency triples and it begins returning timeouts on about 4% of calls. The on-call architect must decide the failure behaviour before the next storm window. What should the design do?

options.A: Move moderation off the synchronous path entirely and classify stored transcripts asynchronously, raising an alert whenever a violation is found after delivery; nothing in the request path then depends on the classifier.
options.B: Fail open on both paths and write the unmoderated turns to the incident log for next-day review, because blocking a customer who is reporting a gas smell is the larger harm.
options.C: Fail closed on both paths and serve a maintenance notice until the classifier recovers, so that no unmoderated content can reach a customer during any period when the utility cannot verify what it is saying.
options.D: Bind the failure behaviour to each path's risk: the free-text safety path fails closed to a scripted response carrying the emergency number, while the deterministic status lookup keeps serving.

items.question: A manufacturer's procurement assistant ingests supplier PDFs — quotes, spec sheets, terms — into a retrieval index and has three tools: `search_documents`, `get_contract_terms`, and `create_purchase_order`. During an internal exercise, a document uploaded through the supplier portal contained a paragraph addressed to the assistant telling it to raise a purchase order, and the assistant did so. The team has to close this before the portal opens to 4,000 suppliers. What is the primary architectural fix?

options.A: Add a system-prompt directive, repeated ahead of each retrieved passage, telling the assistant that any instruction inside a supplier document is not from the buyer and must be ignored.
options.B: Run an injection-detection classifier over every ingested document and quarantine flagged files before they reach the index, so hostile content is stopped at the portal rather than discovered afterwards in a raised purchase order.
options.C: Strip imperative sentences and second-person phrasing from document text during ingestion, so that no instruction-shaped content is ever indexed and the assistant retrieves only declarative material from supplier files.
options.D: Treat all document text as data with no authority, and require `create_purchase_order` to be authorised by a deterministic check outside the model that matches the order against an originating buyer request.

items.question: In an indirect prompt-injection defence, what does wrapping retrieved passages in explicit untrusted-content markers actually buy you?

options.A: It causes the tokeniser to exclude the marked spans from attention, so the delimited content still contributes context without being able to influence what the model generates.
options.B: It is the mechanism that lets the model attribute each claim to the correct source document when it produces citations alongside a retrieved answer.
options.C: It prevents the model from acting on instructions embedded in the passages, so tool-layer authorisation checks on consequential actions become redundant.
options.D: It lowers the probability that embedded text is treated as instruction, but remains a probabilistic mitigation, so authorisation must still be enforced outside the model.

items.question: An HR SaaS vendor ships an assistant that answers employee questions about their own pay, leave and benefits. It reaches the HR system through a single service account with read access to every record across all customer tenants, and the current design injects the requesting employee's ID into the system prompt with an instruction to only discuss that person. A penetration test showed the assistant returning a colleague's salary band when the tester phrased the question as a comparison. What change addresses the root cause?

options.A: Strengthen the system prompt with an explicit rule that the assistant may discuss only the requesting employee's own record and must refuse all comparative questions.
options.B: Add an output filter that detects employee names and compensation figures, blocking any response that contains a name other than the requester's before it is returned to the browser.
options.C: Issue a unique session identifier for each conversation and log every HR query made under it, so that any unauthorised disclosure can afterwards be traced to a specific session and user.
options.D: Exchange the employee's authenticated session for a scoped, on-behalf-of credential and enforce record-level entitlements inside the HR data service that fetches the record.

items.question: A revenue-cycle vendor summarises clinical notes for hospital coders. The summary is written back into the EHR and must carry the real patient name, MRN and admitting physician so the coder can act on it. Legal wants direct identifiers kept out of the model call. The team is choosing an identifier-handling design for a pipeline processing 90,000 notes a night. Which design meets both requirements?

options.A: Send the real identifiers and rely on the contractual commitment that customer data is not used to train models, which is the assurance the vendor agreement already provides for this pipeline.
options.B: Replace each direct identifier with a generic placeholder such as `[PATIENT]` or `[MRN]` before the call and instruct the model to preserve the placeholders in its output.
options.C: Hash each identifier with a per-patient salt so the model receives a stable, non-reversible token that stays consistent across every note belonging to the same patient.
options.D: Tokenise identifiers through a vault held outside the model boundary, send the surrogate tokens in the call, and re-hydrate the surrogates in the returned summary before it is written to the EHR.

items.question: A retailer's support widget renders the assistant's markdown as HTML in the customer's browser, because the product requires clickable product links, tables and inline images from the catalogue. The assistant also summarises the customer's order history and previous ticket text, some of which is attacker-controllable through a returns form. A security review flags the rendering step. What is the correct control?

options.A: Sanitise the generated output server-side against an allowlist of permitted elements and attributes, and resolve every image and link host against a domain allowlist before it is returned.
options.B: Add a system-prompt rule forbidding the assistant from emitting raw HTML, script tags or inline event handlers, and requiring it to stay inside the widget's markdown subset.
options.C: Escape the output entirely and render it as plain text, removing the whole class of markup problem at source and leaving nothing for an injected fragment to act on in the browser.
options.D: Rely on a strict Content Security Policy on the widget page, with `script-src 'self'` and `frame-ancestors 'none'`, since the browser then governs what the page is permitted to load.

items.question: A legal research firm runs an agent over a corpus of case filings, client emails and opposing-counsel submissions, all uploaded by external parties. The agent can search the corpus, draft memos, and send drafts to a named recipient. Counsel wants indirect-injection risk reduced before the agent is enabled for litigation matters. Which three belong in that defence as controls the firm can actually rely on? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: Wrap every retrieved passage in explicit untrusted-content markers with its source and uploader, and instruct the model that marked content is material to analyse and never an instruction to follow.
options.B: Move the agent from Sonnet to Opus, since the higher-capability tier is measurably better at recognising injected instructions inside retrieved material and disregarding them in favour of the lawyer's actual request.
options.C: Require an out-of-band confirmation from the matter owner before any send action executes, independent of what the retrieved material says.
options.D: Enforce the requesting lawyer's matter-level entitlements at the tool layer, so a compromised turn cannot reach filings or recipients the lawyer could not reach directly.
options.E: Raise retrieval top_k substantially so that legitimate passages outnumber any injected one and dilute its influence on what the model generates for the memo.

items.question: A pharmaceutical analytics team gives researchers a Claude assistant that writes and runs Python against internal trial datasets in an execution sandbox. The main concern raised in review is that generated code could send dataset contents out of the environment. Which sandbox control addresses that concern most directly?

options.A: Run the interpreter process as an unprivileged non-root user inside the container, so that generated code cannot escalate privileges, install system packages, or modify any file owned by the runtime environment itself.
options.B: Deny all outbound network traffic from the sandbox by default with an explicit allowlist for the few required internal hosts, and inject no ambient cloud or database credentials into the runtime.
options.C: Run a static analyser over every generated script and refuse to execute anything that references sockets, networking or file-transfer libraries before the code reaches the interpreter.
options.D: Apply per-execution CPU, memory and wall-clock limits enforced by the container runtime, so one researcher's runaway job cannot exhaust the shared analytics pool.

items.question: A gaming company streams assistant responses into an in-client chat panel; product measures time-to-first-token as a headline KPI and will not accept a non-streamed experience. The output moderation classifier they use needs a coherent span of text to score reliably and returns noisy verdicts on very short fragments. Moderation must prevent violating content reaching players, not merely record it. How should the streaming path be built?

options.A: Emit tokens to the client as they arrive and pull the message from the chat panel with a retraction event if a post-hoc classification of the completed response flags it.
options.B: Disable streaming and return complete, fully classified responses, accepting the regression in time-to-first-token as the unavoidable cost of a control that must prevent rather than record.
options.C: Classify only the opening segment of each response, since a completion that is going to violate policy almost always declares itself in its first sentences, and scanning less keeps the added delay off the streaming path.
options.D: Hold a rolling buffer, classify each completed segment together with a short overlap from the previous one, and release only cleared segments; on a violation, stop generation and replace the whole message with a safe notice.

items.question: A wealth advisory firm indexes client statements, meeting notes and suitability assessments into one vector store shared by all advisers. Advisers are restricted to their own book of clients, and an internal audit has asked how that restriction is enforced in the assistant. The current implementation retrieves the top 20 chunks for the query and then discards any belonging to clients outside the adviser's book before building the prompt. What should change?

options.A: Derive an entitlement filter from the adviser's authenticated identity and apply it as a pre-filter in the vector query.
options.B: Keep the global retrieval and post-filter, but raise the candidate set to 100 chunks so enough in-book material survives filtering to answer the question.
options.C: Add a system-prompt instruction naming the adviser's client list explicitly and forbidding any discussion of a client who does not appear on it, refreshed at the start of every session.
options.D: Encrypt each client's documents with a per-client key, so unauthorised content cannot be read even in the event that the retrieval step happens to return it.

items.question: A media company is deploying a Haiku-based classifier as an input guardrail in front of its editorial assistant, replacing a regex list. The safety lead asks what the deployment needs beyond the classifier itself to be operable. Which two properties should the design have? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: The classifier call carries its own timeout and retry policy, with an explicitly defined behaviour when it exceeds them, independent of the main generation call's settings.
options.B: The classifier is given the same system prompt as the editorial assistant so that it evaluates each input with full knowledge of the product's purpose, tone and editorial standards.
options.C: Every decision is recorded with the score, the threshold in force and a reference to the input, so thresholds can be re-tuned against real traffic and reviewed after incidents.
options.D: The decision threshold is fixed at whatever value maximises overall accuracy on the validation set, so that the classifier operates at its best measured performance point across the set as a whole.
options.E: The classifier runs only when the editorial assistant's response is a refusal, avoiding cost on the majority of traffic that is clearly benign.

items.question: A travel platform's support agent handles 60% of contacts end-to-end and can call `cancel_booking`, `rebook`, and `issue_refund`. It also has an itinerary-import feature that parses customer-forwarded confirmation emails, which are arbitrary attacker-influenced HTML. A support ticket this morning shows the agent cancelled a booking the customer never mentioned, immediately after processing an imported email. Traces confirm the cancellation followed content in the imported message. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.A: Deploy a system-prompt update instructing the agent that content inside imported emails is data and must never be treated as a request, and monitor for recurrence.
options.B: Revoke the mutating tool scopes for any session that has processed imported content, leaving import read-only and the rest of the agent's contact handling intact, while the design fix is built.
options.C: Take the agent offline for all contacts until an injection-detection classifier has been trained on imported-email traffic and deployed in front of the parser, so nothing resumes until the vector is provably closed.
options.D: Queue a batch job to find other bookings cancelled shortly after an import, notify affected customers, and schedule a design review for the next sprint.

items.question: Which failure mode can be caught by an output-side guardrail but not by an input-side one?

options.A: A user asks outright for content in a category the product has decided it will not serve under any circumstances.
options.B: A benign question makes the response repeat another customer's record that retrieval placed in context.
options.C: A request arrives whose fully assembled prompt exceeds the token budget the system has configured for that particular route.
options.D: A user pastes a widely circulated jailbreak template into their message before stating the request they actually want fulfilled.

items.question: A telco's observability pipeline captures full prompts and completions for every assistant turn as span attributes, and those spans go to a hosted vendor. Prompts contain subscriber names, account numbers and, in porting cases, addresses. The privacy team requires that personal data not leave the telco's boundary in telemetry, while engineering needs to keep debugging multi-step failures across services. Which two changes meet both requirements? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Redact identified entities in the emitting service before the span is exported, so raw values never leave the process that held them.
options.B: Enable the observability vendor's ingest-time scrubbing rules as the control, since they apply uniformly across every service and language in the pipeline.
options.C: Shorten trace retention so telemetry is short-lived enough that redaction is not required.
options.D: Emit a stable salted hash in place of each redacted entity, so the same subscriber can still be correlated across spans and services during debugging.
options.E: Sample 1% of traces so the great majority of prompts are never persisted at all.

items.question: A schools tutoring product classifies every incoming student message independently and blocks on a per-message score. Safety review finds sessions where each individual message scored well under threshold, yet the conversation as a whole walked the assistant from a history lesson into content the product must never produce for minors. Message-level scores show a slow upward drift across ten to fifteen turns but never cross the line. What change addresses this?

options.A: Score at the conversation level — run the guardrail over a rolling window of recent turns and keep a per-session risk score that escalates when the trajectory, not any single message, crosses a threshold.
options.B: Lower the per-message threshold so the drifting messages are caught earlier in the sequence, well before the conversation has travelled far enough for the content to become genuinely unsuitable for a school setting or reach a student.
options.C: Re-inject the full safety system prompt before every turn and pin it after the conversation history, so the model's standing instructions cannot be diluted by the accumulating transcript.
options.D: Cap conversations at twenty turns and force a fresh session with a cleared transcript once the cap is reached, so that no single exchange can accumulate enough momentum to drift.

items.question: A logistics operator is hardening a dispatch agent used by 900 depot staff. Today it has one broad `manage_shipment` tool that reads and mutates, and it reaches the shipments database using the same credential as the main dispatch web application. Which three changes move the design toward least privilege in a way that is actually enforced? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: Split `manage_shipment` into separate read and mutate tools, so the mutating one can carry a stricter authorisation path and be withheld from roles that only need lookups.
options.B: Put the authorisation rules in the system prompt in structured form, so the agent can decline out-of-scope requests before it ever calls a tool.
options.C: Resolve the acting identity from the authenticated session and have the tool layer re-check authorisation against it, rather than trusting a staff identifier supplied in the tool arguments.
options.D: Give the agent its own database credential scoped to the specific tables and operations its tools require, instead of reusing the dispatch application's credential.
options.E: Keep the single broad credential for operational simplicity and log every tool invocation with its arguments for weekly review.

items.question: A grocery retailer's loyalty support assistant answers questions about points balances and voucher eligibility. The current implementation fetches the full customer profile object — including date of birth, address history, payment tokens and purchase history — and pastes it into the prompt because it was the simplest thing the existing API returned. Privacy review asks for a change. What should the team do?

options.A: Continue sending the full profile but place it behind a prompt cache breakpoint so the record is transmitted once rather than on every turn.
options.B: Continue sending the full profile but add a system-prompt instruction that the assistant must ignore fields not relevant to the question asked.
options.C: Continue sending the full profile and add an output filter that removes any personal field appearing in the assistant's response before it is shown to the customer.
options.D: Build a server-side projection that returns only the fields the loyalty task needs — points balance, tier, voucher eligibility flags — and send that.

items.question: A recruitment platform's screening assistant fetches each candidate's portfolio URL, reads the page, and writes an assessment note into the applicant tracking system for recruiters to read. The page content is entirely candidate-controlled. Security has raised that a candidate could shape their page to manipulate the note written about them. The team must keep the feature. What is the right structure?

options.A: Keep the raw page text in the assistant's context but bracket it with a warning, repeated after the passage, that the content is candidate-supplied and must never be treated as instruction.
options.B: Fetch only URLs on domains the candidate has verified by email and that present a valid certificate, so the origin of the content is confirmed before the assistant is permitted to read it.
options.C: Feed the fetched page to a constrained extraction call that returns only a fixed schema of factual fields, validate the result against that schema, and let the assessment step see only the validated structure.
options.D: Run the fetched page through the same HTML sanitiser the product uses when rendering assistant output to recruiters, so the page is neutralised by a control the team has already built and tested.

items.question: A hospital group's referral intake handles about 2,000 external referral letters a day, arriving as emailed PDFs from practices outside its control. An agent reads each letter and books an appointment in the scheduling system, which it can write to directly. Clinical governance will not accept a design where letter content can steer a booking, and the volume rules out clinician confirmation of every extracted field. How should the components be arranged?

options.A: Give the planning agent the raw letter text but restrict its tool set to create and amend operations on the scheduling system only, so the worst case is a mis-booked appointment.
options.B: Send the letter to two different models in parallel and proceed only when their extractions agree, treating any disagreement as a signal that the document may have been tampered with.
options.C: Have the agent present every extracted field to the intake clerk for confirmation before the booking call is made, so a human always stands between the letter and the scheduling system whatever the letter contains.
options.D: Route the letter to a reader model that has no tools and returns only typed values, and have the privileged planner work from those values as opaque variables without ever receiving the letter text.

items.question: A publishing group connects its editorial agent to a third-party MCP server for digital asset management, alongside its own internal MCP servers for the CMS and the rights database. During review, an architect notes that the third-party server supplies its tool names, descriptions and JSON schemas at connection time, that these strings are placed into the model's context, and that the vendor can change them in any release. What control addresses this exposure?

options.A: Snapshot the server's tool manifest — names, descriptions and schemas — into version control at review time, diff it on every connection, and refuse any tool whose definition changed without re-approval.
options.B: Instruct the agent in its system prompt that tool names, descriptions and parameter docs are metadata only, and that any instruction-like text found within them must be disregarded.
options.C: Connect to the third-party server over stdio rather than HTTP, so the manifest travels over a local transport that cannot be intercepted or modified in flight by a network attacker.
options.D: Expose only the third-party server's read-only tools, on the basis that a tool which cannot mutate state cannot cause harm however its description is worded or whenever the vendor chooses to change it between releases.

items.question: A claims assistant at a motor insurer reads adjuster notes and third-party repair-shop reports, then proposes actions: request further evidence, approve a settlement below a threshold, or escalate. Repair-shop reports are supplied by external garages. The team wants a detection layer that catches the case where the proposed action does not match what the claim handler actually asked for. What should they build?

options.A: Add a follow-up turn in the same conversation asking the assistant to re-read the shop report, its own proposed action and the handler's request, then confirm the three are consistent.
options.B: Embed a unique canary string in the system prompt and block any response in which that canary appears, on the basis that a turn which has been redirected will usually surface the instructions it was originally given.
options.C: Log every proposed action and raise an alert whenever the rate of settlement approvals rises above the rolling baseline for that handler's team, so a manipulated pattern surfaces within the day.
options.D: Run a separate check that receives only the handler's original request and the proposed action — not the notes or the shop report — and must judge the action to be within what was asked before it executes.

items.question: Compared with direct prompt injection, what makes indirect injection through retrieved documents structurally harder to defend against?

options.A: Retrieved text is tokenised differently from user-authored text, which makes it materially harder for a classifier to score the retrieved portion accurately.
options.B: The payload arrives through a channel the system itself chose to fetch and trust, so there is no user-supplied message to screen and the content can have been planted long before any request.
options.C: Indirect injection only affects agents with tool access, because the payload needs a tool call to have any effect, and tool-calling paths cannot be sandboxed the way generation can.
options.D: Direct injection is reliably prevented by model training, so the indirect variant is now the only one that still reaches production systems and therefore the only one worth designing controls against.

items.question: A university admissions office scores 40,000 free-text personal statements. Policy requires that direct identifiers and volunteered health disclosures be removed before the text reaches the scoring model. An engineer proposes an extra Claude call that redacts the statement, whose output is then passed to the scoring call. The privacy officer rejects the design. What is the substantive problem, and what should replace it?

options.A: Nothing is fundamentally wrong with the design; it is acceptable provided the redaction call runs on the cheaper Haiku tier, which keeps the additional cost proportionate at forty thousand statements.
options.B: The problem is that the pipeline now makes two calls per statement, doubling both latency and spend; route the redaction pass through batch processing so the extra work happens off the critical path.
options.C: The redaction call transmits the unredacted statement across exactly the boundary the control exists to protect, so it removes no exposure; run detection inside the trust boundary with a dedicated detector instead.
options.D: The problem is that a generative redactor can invent replacement text that is not in the original; set temperature to zero and pin the model version so every statement redacts identically on re-run.

items.question: A developer-tools company builds an operations agent that proposes remediation steps and hands them to a runner that executes them on infrastructure hosts. Today the agent emits free-form shell command strings and the runner executes them. Which two changes make execution defensible? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Escape shell metacharacters in the generated command string before handing it to the shell, so that no unexpected token can change how the command is parsed at execution time.
options.B: Replace free-form command generation with a fixed catalogue of parameterised operations that the agent selects by name, with every argument validated against a declared schema and value range.
options.C: Require the agent to emit a plain-language explanation of each command that the on-call engineer must read and acknowledge before execution proceeds on the host.
options.D: Execute in an ephemeral container that holds no ambient credentials and denies outbound network traffic by default, so an operation that slips past validation cannot reach production systems.
options.E: Require commands to be emitted as JSON objects rather than raw strings, so the runner can parse them reliably before execution.

items.question: A multi-tenant analytics SaaS lets an assistant generate and run data transformations against each customer's uploaded datasets. Execution happens in a sandbox. Which sandbox lifecycle design best limits blast radius between customers?

options.A: A warm pool of long-lived sandboxes shared across all tenants, with working files deleted between runs to remove any residue.
options.B: A fresh, ephemeral sandbox per execution, destroyed afterwards, with no state shared across runs or tenants.
options.C: One sandbox per tenant, kept warm for the whole of that tenant's session and shared by all of that tenant's analysts and scheduled jobs.
options.D: A single shared sandbox with a separate directory per tenant and operating-system file permissions separating one tenant's working area from another's.

items.question: A public-sector open-data portal offers a natural-language query feature over published statistical views; its whole value proposition is arbitrary ad-hoc analytical queries, so a fixed set of canned reports would not serve the use case. The assistant generates SQL, which the application currently screens with a regular expression rejecting `DROP`, `DELETE` and `UPDATE`, then executes using the portal's application database credential. What should replace this?

options.A: Extend the deny-list to cover more dangerous keywords, and add detection for stacked statements, comment markers and the other constructs historically used to slip past keyword screening, leaving the existing execution path unchanged.
options.B: Have the assistant emit a structured query description that the application compiles into SQL, so that no model-generated SQL is ever executed against the database at all.
options.C: Execute the generated SQL unchanged but log every statement and have a data analyst review a 5% sample each morning, so misuse against the published views is detected within a working day.
options.D: Parse the generated SQL into a syntax tree, allowlist the constructs and objects it may reference, and execute it under a read-only role scoped to the published views with a statement timeout and a row cap.

items.question: A health insurer's member chat deployed a retuned input classifier at 22:00. By 07:00 the deflection-to-human rate has tripled and the contact centre is saturated; hold times are past their published service commitment. Sampling ten blocked messages shows ordinary questions about claim status and prescription coverage. The safety team believes the new threshold is responsible but has not proven it. What should happen next?

options.A: Disable the input guardrail entirely until the analysis is complete, since the service ran without it for months before this release and recorded no incident in that period.
options.B: Leave the threshold in place and surge contact-centre capacity with overtime and overflow agents while the safety team gathers a statistically adequate sample of blocked messages.
options.C: Revert the threshold to its previous value — a configuration change that restores known behaviour within minutes — then analyse a sample of the newly blocked messages against both the old and new verdicts.
options.D: Relabel the newly blocked messages as benign, retrain the classifier on the corrected set, and redeploy once evaluation on the labelled holdout shows the regression has been eliminated and hold times can recover.

items.question: A motor insurer extracts repair line items from claim packs using vision input. Each pack is a scanned PDF containing the repair invoice, the policyholder's correspondence, bank details for the payout, and damage photographs. Only the invoice line items are needed for the extraction task. Which two measures genuinely reduce the personal data reaching the model? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Downscale every page image to the lowest resolution at which extraction still succeeds, since fewer pixels means less personal data transmitted.
options.B: Mask the regions of the invoice that the task does not use — the correspondence address block and the bank detail panel — before the image is sent.
options.C: Instruct the model in the prompt to attend only to the line-item table and disregard all other content on the page.
options.D: Select only the invoice pages using a deterministic page classifier and send those, rather than submitting the whole claim pack.
options.E: Retain the submitted images for 90 days so extraction can be re-run if the claim is later disputed.

items.question: A travel company's assistant serves customers in thirty languages. Its input guardrail was trained and tuned on English. Abuse analysis finds attempts that the input classifier scores as benign — some arriving in languages with little representation in the classifier's training data, some arriving in an encoded form — while the model still understands them and, in a small number of cases, responded inappropriately. The team must close the coverage gap without a language-by-language build-out. Which change most reliably closes it?

options.A: Score the model's response with an output guardrail operating in the language the response is produced in, whatever form the request took.
options.B: Add a decoding pre-pass that reverses every encoding the team can enumerate and re-scores the decoded text with the same English-tuned classifier.
options.C: Reject any message the language detector does not identify as one of the thirty supported languages, so that unscored input never reaches the model at all.
options.D: Commission a separately tuned classifier for each of the thirty supported languages, so guardrail coverage matches the product's full language footprint rather than only its largest markets.

items.question: A field-service company's technician assistant carries 40 tools spanning parts ordering, warranty claims, scheduling, customer records and equipment telemetry. Any given job uses three or four of them. A review notes that a manipulated turn can currently reach all 40, and that the tool block also consumes a large share of the context budget. What is the strongest change?

options.A: Have a deterministic router classify the incoming job into a workflow and expose only that workflow's tool subset for the turn, so the reachable surface is bounded in code.
options.B: Keep all 40 tools available and describe the current job phase in the system prompt, listing the tools appropriate to that phase, so the assistant selects only from them.
options.C: Consolidate the 40 tools into 12 more general tools, each taking a mode parameter that selects the specific operation, which also shrinks the tool block considerably.
options.D: Keep all 40 tools available but require an explicit confirmation step before any of them executes, so that no tool call reaches a downstream system without a technician having agreed to it in the field.

items.question: A software company's IT service-desk agent can reset passwords, install approved software, grant group membership and provision cloud roles. Every action currently routes to a human approver. Telemetry shows 98% of approvals are granted within eight seconds of arriving, and a spot check finds approvers rarely open the detail view. The security lead wants the approval control to mean something again. What should change?

options.A: Keep universal approval and address the behaviour with approver training, a target minimum review time, and dashboards showing per-approver decision latency and detail-view open rate against that target.
options.B: Remove approvals altogether and rely on comprehensive post-hoc audit logging plus a fast rollback capability for every action type, since a control nobody reads provides no assurance anyway and costs real time.
options.C: Tier actions by reversibility and privilege impact: auto-execute reversible low-impact actions with logging, and route only privilege-granting or irreversible ones to approval with the parameters shown.
options.D: Route each approval to the requesting user's line manager instead of the shared service-desk queue, so the approver knows the requester's role, cost centre and current project.

items.question: You are reviewing an agent design for a fleet-leasing business ahead of a security sign-off. Which three characteristics indicate a confused-deputy exposure? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: The agent issues several tool calls in parallel within a turn, so multiple privileged operations against downstream systems are in flight at the same moment.
options.B: The agent authenticates to downstream systems with a shared service identity whose permissions are the union of all users' permissions.
options.C: The identity the tool layer authorises against is taken from a field in the model's tool-call arguments rather than derived from the authenticated session.
options.D: Tool results are returned to the model as JSON documents rather than as prose summaries written by an intermediate formatting step before the model reads them.
options.E: Content the agent retrieves from external sources can determine which record a privileged tool operates on, with no independent check against the user's request.

items.question: An agent's responses may contain links and images, and its tools can make outbound HTTP requests. Why enforce a destination allowlist on both?

options.A: It lowers response latency by avoiding DNS resolution for hosts the system has not previously seen and cached, which matters on long agent runs.
options.B: It ensures the agent attributes each claim to the correct source when it cites material, because only allowlisted hosts can appear in the citations it produces.
options.C: It guarantees that every URL the agent produces resolves to a live page rather than a broken link, so users are never sent to a destination that no longer exists.
options.D: It prevents attacker-influenced content from turning a link, an image load or a fetch into a channel that carries context data to a destination the operator never chose.

items.question: An online marketplace's seller-support assistant currently makes a single block-or-allow decision across all its content categories. Product and safety agree that some categories warrant a hard block, some are better served by a safe response pointing to a support resource, and some should reach a human specialist. How should the guardrail be restructured?

options.A: Apply the action required by the most severe category uniformly across every category, so that nothing is ever under-handled and the policy remains simple to state and to audit.
options.B: Map each category to a severity tier with an action per tier: hard block, safe response with a resource, or route to a human specialist.
options.C: Keep the binary block-or-allow decision and lower the single threshold so borderline seller messages fall on the block side rather than reaching the assistant.
options.D: Let the assistant decide the appropriate action in-prompt, based on the category it identifies in the request, so that policy and generation stay in one place and a change needs only a single edit.

items.question: An airline's service assistant has run an input and output guardrail stack for six months. The safety lead can currently report only the daily block count and wants a measurement approach that would actually reveal degradation. Which two practices provide that? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Track the absolute number of blocked requests per day as the primary health metric for the guardrail stack, alerting whenever it moves outside its usual range.
options.B: Maintain a labelled holdout of adversarial and benign cases, re-run it on every guardrail change, and report false-negative and false-positive rates separately.
options.C: Track the mean classifier confidence score across all classified requests and alert whenever that mean shifts away from its established baseline over a rolling week.
options.D: Sample allowed traffic for periodic human review, so false negatives — which generate no signal of their own — are estimated rather than assumed to be zero.
options.E: Track the proportion of requests routed to the higher-capability model tier as a proxy for how often difficult content is arriving at the assistant.

items.question: A legal-tech SaaS serves 200 law firms through a single gateway service that holds one API credential for all tenants. To cut cost the team wants to use prompt caching. The proposed prefix, assembled from a shared template, is: platform instructions, then the firm's practice-area policy, then a matter summary containing privileged client facts. A reviewer worries about cross-firm exposure through the cache. How should the prefix and the gateway be arranged?

options.A: Place only tenant-neutral platform instructions and shared policy before the cache breakpoint, keep firm and matter content after it, and scope cache identity per tenant rather than pooling it.
options.B: Cache the full per-firm prefix including the matter summary, relying on the requirement that a prefix must match exactly for a cache hit to occur, which makes each firm's prefix effectively unique.
options.C: Disable caching on any request containing client data and accept the resulting cost increase as the unavoidable price of keeping privileged material out of shared infrastructure.
options.D: Append the firm identifier to the end of the prompt so that every firm's request is textually distinct, which keeps one firm's cached content from being reachable by another firm's call through the shared gateway.

items.question: A supply-chain platform runs an orchestrator that delegates supplier due-diligence research to a subagent. The subagent browses supplier websites and public registries, then returns a findings block. The orchestrator reads that block and can flag a supplier, release a hold, or open a payment run. A design review asks how injected content on a supplier's own site is prevented from steering the orchestrator. What is the correct principle to apply?

options.A: Treat the subagent's findings block as trusted, since the subagent runs inside the platform boundary under the same system prompt, the same safety policies and the same model version as the orchestrator.
options.B: Label each subagent result with the trust level of the lowest-trust input that contributed to it, and require the orchestrator to apply untrusted-content handling and authorisation checks to anything so labelled.
options.C: Run the research subagent on the higher-capability model tier, since it is the component directly exposed to hostile supplier pages and registry text and benefits most from stronger judgement.
options.D: Have the subagent paraphrase its findings into its own prose before returning them, so that any injected wording is rewritten in the subagent's voice rather than passed through verbatim to the orchestrator.

items.question: A national tax agency's contact-centre assistant has been in production for a year. The team wants a regression corpus built from real transcripts, because the failures worth guarding against are ones synthetic cases have not reproduced. Transcripts contain taxpayer identifiers, income figures and family circumstances. The eval corpus will live in the ML team's repository and be read by contractors. How should the corpus be produced and held?

options.A: Copy the transcripts into the eval repository unchanged and restrict access with a repository access-control list naming the ML team and the individual contractors cleared to read it.
options.B: Abandon real transcripts and generate a wholly synthetic corpus mirroring the observed failure categories, so the regression suite reproduces the behaviours the team cares about without taxpayer data leaving production.
options.C: Copy the transcripts unchanged but set a 30-day expiry on the eval corpus and purge the repository's history on each rotation, so any exposure created by the copy is bounded in time.
options.D: De-identify at extraction with the production path's detector, verify with a sampled re-identification check, and hold the corpus under the source classification and retention rules until it passes.

items.question: An e-commerce operations agent calls internal and third-party APIs. Several third parties return verbose error bodies that echo request content and include free-text remediation guidance authored by the provider. These bodies are currently passed into the model's context verbatim as tool results. Which two changes reduce the injection surface? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Truncate every tool result to a fixed character budget so no single result can dominate the context window.
options.B: Map upstream failures to an enumerated set of internal error codes with a bounded message drawn from a fixed vocabulary, and return that to the model instead of the provider's raw body.
options.C: Retry every failed tool call up to three times before surfacing any error to the model, so transient faults never reach it.
options.D: Apply the same untrusted-content marking and provenance labelling to tool results as the system already applies to retrieved documents.
options.E: Convert tool results from JSON into prose before adding them to the context so the model parses them more reliably.

items.question: A music streaming service has built a new output guardrail for its artist-support assistant. It performs well on the team's labelled set, but has never seen production traffic and the team has no estimate of its false-positive rate on real requests. A wrongful block is user-visible and the assistant handles a large share of artist queries. The change is built and merged behind a flag. What should the team do next?

options.A: Enable enforcement globally at a deliberately conservative threshold and monitor the daily block rate, tightening it in a later release once real traffic data is available to tune against.
options.B: Enable enforcement for a random 5% of users and compare their support-contact rate against the remaining 95%, using the difference as the estimate of how often the guardrail is blocking legitimate requests.
options.C: Run it in monitor-only mode on live traffic, recording verdicts without acting on them, until false-positive and false-negative rates on real traffic are characterised — then enable enforcement, ramped by cohort.
options.D: Enable it and rely on artist support tickets and in-product feedback to surface false positives, since real complaints from affected users are the most reliable signal of over-blocking.

items.question: In an output policy, what is a safe completion, and when is it preferred over a hard refusal?

options.A: A response that withholds the problematic element while still serving the legitimate part of the request; preferred where most requests in the category are benign and refusal blocks real needs.
options.B: A response generated by a smaller, cheaper model after the primary model declines; preferred where latency and cost matter more than the depth of the answer given.
options.C: A refusal accompanied by the text of the policy clause that triggered it; preferred where the organisation needs an auditable record of each individual decision it declined.
options.D: A pre-approved fixed response returned without any model call at all; preferred wherever the organisation needs the wording to be identical every time and independent of what the model would generate.

items.question: A payroll provider's assistant produces JSON payloads for an adjustments API. Payloads are validated against a JSON Schema before dispatch. An incident review finds a payload that passed schema validation and applied an adjustment to an employee outside the requesting administrator's company, at an amount above that employee's per-period cap — a cap that varies by contract and cannot be expressed as a static range. What should be added?

options.A: A deterministic business-rule layer between schema validation and dispatch that checks administrator authority, employee company membership and the contract-derived cap.
options.B: Tighter JSON Schema constraints, including a maximum on the amount field, an enum on the adjustment type and a stricter pattern on the employee identifier so malformed values are rejected.
options.C: A requirement that the assistant name the payroll policy rule permitting the adjustment, with the named rule looked up in the policy document and confirmed to exist before dispatch.
options.D: Routing every adjustment above the median historical amount to human review before dispatch, so that unusually large changes always receive a second pair of eyes before they reach payroll.

items.question: A platform team is building a deployment assistant. An engineer proposes pasting the target service's environment variables — which include database passwords and third-party API tokens — into the assistant's context so it can construct correct deployment commands. What should the design do instead?

options.A: Include the variables but annotate the sensitive ones with a `secret` marker so the assistant knows which values it must never echo back to the engineer.
options.B: Include the variables and add an output filter that redacts anything matching known token and password formats before the response is displayed to the engineer.
options.C: Keep secret values out of the context: expose them to the model as named handles that the tool layer resolves at call time.
options.D: Include the variables but shorten the rotation period sharply, so any secret disclosed through the assistant is valid only briefly and the misuse window stays small.

items.question: A customer-support platform hosts assistants for 60 consumer brands on shared infrastructure. To improve answers over time, the agent writes 'learned facts' distilled from conversation summaries into a memory store and retrieves from it on later turns. A tester using Brand A's assistant received a sentence describing an internal escalation process that only appears in Brand B's documentation. What change addresses this?

options.A: Partition the memory store by tenant, apply the caller's entitlement filter to memory retrieval as to document retrieval, and gate writes so tenant-specific detail is not persisted.
options.B: Keep a single shared store but prefix each entry with its source tenant identifier and instruct the agent to use only entries whose prefix matches the brand it is currently serving.
options.C: Expire memory entries after 30 days, so that any cross-tenant contamination is bounded in time and the store cannot accumulate an indefinite history of one brand's operational detail for another to find.
options.D: Store memory entries as embeddings rather than as text, so the original wording of a brand's internal escalation process cannot be reconstructed by reading the store.

items.question: A research consortium runs an assistant over a corpus that mixes staff-curated collections with documents contributed by 3,000 external member institutions. Some assistant workflows feed grant-eligibility decisions. Which three ingestion-side measures meaningfully reduce the risk from deliberately planted content? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: Record provenance for every chunk — contributing institution, source system, ingestion timestamp — and carry it into the prompt so the origin of retrieved content is visible at generation time.
options.B: Screen contributed documents at ingestion with an injection-pattern detector and route flagged items to human review before they are indexed.
options.C: Separate the index by trust level, so workflows feeding eligibility decisions retrieve only from the staff-curated collection.
options.D: Re-embed the entire corpus nightly, so any planted content is re-scored against the current embedding model and loses relevance.
options.E: Store contributed documents in a write-once archive so their content cannot be altered after ingestion.

items.question: A market-research firm redacts personal data from open-ended survey responses before they are processed by an assistant and shared with client analysts. The detector's measured recall on a labelled internal set is 0.94. The delivery lead wants to describe the output to clients as 'personal data removed'. What is the correct engineering position?

options.A: Raise the detector's sensitivity until recall on the labelled set reaches 1.0, at which point the description becomes accurate and the delivery lead's wording can stand without qualification to a client or an audit.
options.B: Treat the redacted corpus as still containing personal data: keep its classification and access controls, add an independent output-side scan, and report the measured recall rather than claiming removal.
options.C: Run a second detector from a different vendor in series over the same responses, and treat agreement between the two on a given response as evidence that removal there is complete.
options.D: Have an analyst manually review a 1% random sample of the redacted responses and, if that sample is clean, describe the whole corpus as clean to clients on the strength of the sampling.

items.question: A white-label conversational platform lets each of its 800 self-serve customers write their own persona and instruction text through a console. That text is composed into the system prompt alongside the platform's own safety rules. Customers can edit it at any time without review. Security asks how platform safety rules survive a customer whose text attempts to relax or override them. What is the sound design?

options.A: Compose the platform's safety rules after the customer's persona text in the system prompt, and repeat them at the end, so the later instructions take precedence over anything above.
options.B: Require manual review and approval of each customer's prompt text before their assistant is activated, so no unreviewed instruction reaches production and every persona has been read by someone at the platform.
options.C: Run each submitted prompt through the model at save time, asking whether the text attempts to relax or override the platform's safety rules, and reject any submission it flags.
options.D: Validate customer text against a bounded template — length limits, permitted sections, disallowed constructs — and enforce platform safety with guardrails that run outside the model whatever the prompt says.

items.question: Two weeks before launch, a red team shows that content planted in a merchant-controlled field on a parcel record caused a postal operator's tracking assistant to disclose a different customer's delivery address. The record contains several merchant-editable fields. The assistant reaches the tracking service with a shared read credential covering all parcels. The team has capacity for one substantial control before launch. Which should it be?

options.A: Ship an injection-pattern classifier over the merchant-editable fields and exclude flagged parcels from assistant handling until a human has reviewed the record and cleared it for use.
options.B: Strip all merchant-editable fields from parcel records before they reach the assistant, and restore them after launch once a longer-term design has been agreed and implemented.
options.C: Enforce the requesting customer's entitlements inside the tracking data service so the assistant cannot retrieve another customer's record at all, and treat injection hardening as follow-on work.
options.D: Add a system-prompt rule that the assistant may discuss only the requesting customer's own parcels, and log any response that names a different customer or a different delivery address.
